description: Looking forward for an incredible potential terrestrial analog for either the Moon or Mars.
summary: This study proposes Tamia Tehsil in Madhya Pradesh, India, as an accessible terrestrial analog for Mars. While current Mars rovers cannot excavate deep into the Martian crust, existing analogs either lack sedimentary interactions (Hawaii, Iceland) or require extreme polar logistics (Antarctica). Using NASA Mars Trek, NASA Planetary Data System (SHARAD) documentation, NASA Photojournal, and NASA Planetary Analog Explorer alongside Google Earth 3D modeling and Google Maps bare-earth terrain shading, this study maps four distinct analog zones across Tamia: the open-air canyon system & natural amphitheater of Patalkot Valley, the Pachmarhi dyke swarm, the Chakhla-Delakhari sill complex, and the basalt-capped Tamia Hills. Here, Deccan Traps flood basalts intruded & interacted directly with soft & cold Gondwana sandstones, exposing a fossilized 3D magmatic plumbing network right at the surface. Beyond mirroring Martian landmarks like Valles Marineris and Cerberus Fossae, Tamia’s basalt-over-sandstone stratigraphy provides a low-cost, road-accessible calibration testbed for subsurface water radar (SHARAD), hydrothermal biosignature detection, and rover mobility.
details:
What Our Project Does & How It Works:
Project Cosmic Linker is a planetary geology and remote-sensing investigation that identifies and evaluates Tamia Tehsil in the Chhindwara district of Madhya Pradesh, India, as a high-value terrestrial planetary analog for Mars. Because planetary scientists or rovers cannot physically excavate through the Martian surface to examine subsurface volcanic-sedimentary structures, we analyzed Tamia Tehsil, where erosion has sliced open a fossilized magmatic plumbing system. Here, in the Tamia Hills, tholeiitic flood basalts of the Deccan Traps intruded and interacted directly with soft and cold Gondwana sandstones. Using multi-platform orbital imagery and bare-earth terrain modeling, this study mapped four distinct Martian analog zones - the open-air canyons and natural amphitheaters of Patalkot Valley, the Pachmarhi dyke swarm, the Chakhla-Delakhari sill complex, and the basalt-capped Tamia Hills - and also conducted a rigorous comparative analysis against Martian landmarks including Valles Marineris and Cerberus Fossae.

Benefits & Intended Mission Impact:
While existing volcanic analogs such as Hawaii and Iceland are basalt-on-basalt, and subsurface plumbing analogs like Antarctica’s McMurdo Dry Valleys require extreme military logistics and environmental treaties, Tamia Tehsil provides a road-accessible, open-air 3D geological testbed. Its primary mission impacts include:

1. Subsurface Water Detection (SHARAD Calibration): In Tamia Hills, impermeable basalt cap-rock traps groundwater inside underlying porous sandstone, creating dielectric contrasts that help calibrate Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO) SHARAD radar for detecting buried ice and water beneath dry Martian basalt.

2. Astrobiological Biosignature Guidance: The cooling 1,200°C basaltic intrusions meeting wet Gondwana sandstones created warm, clay-rich, mineral-dense contact zones - offering astrobiologists an exact mineralogical blueprint for what to search for fossilized Martian microbes.

3. Rover Mobility & Canyon Navigation: Patalkot’s stepped basalt escarpments and sharp canyon walls replicate real Martian rover traversal hazards without extreme polar expedition costs.

Tools, Datasets & Software Used:
• NASA Data & Platforms: NASA Mars Trek (3D Martian terrain and elevation comparisons), NASA Planetary Data System (PDS) MRO SHARAD Archive (subsurface radar attenuation and dielectric contrast principles), NASA Photojournal (high-resolution orbital imagery), and NASA Planetary Analog Explorer (analog qualification criteria).
• Geospatial & Visualization Software: Google Earth (3D perspective modeling and elevation profiling), Google Maps Terrain Layer (bare-earth hill-shading to strip away dense tropical forest canopy).

Creativity & Key Scientific Factors Considered:

Rather than proposing another isolated volcanic crater or desert dune field, our approach creatively leverages bare-earth digital elevation hill-shading to look beneath central India's dense forest canopy and uncover an exposed volcanic-sedimentary plumbing network rarely studied in planetary science. Crucially, to maintain strict scientific integrity, we evaluated both structural similarities (tholeiitic basalt composition, plagioclase-pyroxene mineralogy, dyke-sill geometry) and analog deviations - explicitly accounting for Tamia's humid biosphere, water-driven erosion, zeolite contact metamorphism, and local tectonic scale compared to Mars' hyper-arid vacuum and 266x larger stagnant-lid canyon systems.
